items.title: Athenian democracy excluded most of the population
items.claim: How inclusive was 5th-century BCE Athenian democracy?

options.text: Citizen-men over 18 (perhaps 30,000-40,000) voted in the assembly (ekklesia); women, slaves (perhaps 80,000-100,000) and metics (resident foreigners, perhaps 25,000) had no political rights — citizens were probably 10-20% of the city's population
Women had equal political rights with men

items.reveal:
The Athenian assembly met around 40 times a year on the Pnyx hill. Decisions on war, treaties and major legislation required a quorum of around 6,000. The Council of 500 (boule), juries and most magistracies were filled by lot — a feature of radical democracy.

Pericles' citizenship law (451 BCE) restricted citizenship to those with two Athenian parents. Aristotle's 'Athenaion Politeia' (4th century BCE) describes the system. Thucydides records Pericles' Funeral Oration extolling Athenian democracy in 431 BCE.

Women, even citizen-women, had no vote. Slaves performed much of the manual labour that supported leisure for political participation.
items.why: Calling Athens 'the cradle of democracy' is true with major qualifications. Its political innovations were real and influential — but its exclusions were severe enough that modern democracies share aspirations more than they share institutions with it.

items.title: The NHS opened on 5 July 1948 — over GP opposition
items.claim: Did the medical profession support the founding of the NHS?

options.text: Yes, the BMA welcomed it unanimously
No — most GPs initially opposed it, fearing loss of independence; Aneurin Bevan, Minister of Health, said he had 'stuffed their mouths with gold' by allowing private practice within the NHS

items.reveal:
A 1948 BMA poll found around 90% of doctors opposed to entering the NHS. Bevan negotiated: GPs would be self-employed contractors, not salaried employees; consultants could have NHS posts plus private patients; teaching hospitals retained boards.

The Beveridge Report (1942) had set out the framework — slaying the 'five giants' of want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness. The Labour government (1945-1951) implemented the welfare state. The NHS launched on 5 July 1948, the same day as National Insurance and the National Assistance Act.

Bevan resigned in 1951 over the introduction of prescription charges for dental and optical services.
items.why: Major institutions are rarely born from consensus. The NHS as a 'national treasure' obscures its messy founding — contested, negotiated, and quickly amended.

items.title: Alexander the Great died at 32 with no clear successor
items.claim: What happened to Alexander's empire after his death in 323 BCE?

options.text: It passed peacefully to his infant son

Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 BCE aged 32; his generals (the Diadochi) fought 40 years of wars (323-281 BCE) carving the empire into Hellenistic kingdoms — Ptolemaic Egypt, Seleucid Asia, Antigonid Macedon
It dissolved into independent Greek city-states again

items.reveal:
Alexander had conquered from Macedonia to the Indus in 13 years. Asked on his deathbed who should succeed him, he reportedly said 'to the strongest' (some sources say 'Krateros'). His half-brother Philip III Arrhidaeus (mentally disabled) and posthumous son Alexander IV were both murdered within years.

The Wars of the Diadochi — Antigonus, Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus, Cassander — produced the Hellenistic world that lasted until Rome absorbed it (Macedon 146 BCE, the Seleucid rump 64 BCE, Ptolemaic Egypt 30 BCE).

The Hellenistic kingdoms spread Greek language and culture across western Asia and Egypt — the koine Greek of the New Testament is a downstream consequence.
items.why: Empires built by single conquerors rarely outlast them. Alexander's death at 32 is one of the great 'what ifs' — but his empire's fracture is also a structural fact about charismatic rule without institutional succession.
